outcome: No case of the general Hadwiger dissection conjecture beyond dimension 5 was settled, and no bound moved in this window; the only new 2024-2025 publication in this area re-proves an already-known special case (dissecting an orthoscheme itself into n smaller orthoschemes) rather than advancing the open conjecture about general simplices.
summary: The Hadwiger dissection conjecture (every n-simplex can be dissected into f(n) orthoschemes for some function f) remains open for dimension 6 and above, exactly as it stood on 26 January 2024: proven cases are only dimension 2 (2 orthoschemes), 3 (12), 4 (500), and 5 (~12.5 million). I checked the current Wikipedia article (last edited 27 December 2025 with no citations newer than 2009), the researcher-written survey at florestan.xyz (which discusses the conjecture in detail and mentions no progress past dimension 5, no dimension-6 attempts, and no computational/AI approaches), and searched broadly for any post-2024 arXiv or journal work claiming progress on the general conjecture. None was found. The one 2024-2025 publication I turned up in this space, István Lénárt's 'The Coxeter Trisection and the Hadwiger Conjecture in Multidimensional Spaces' (Journal of Applied Mathematics and Physics, Vol. 12, pp. 4301-4321, Dec 2024, DOI 10.4236/jamp.2024.1212264) and its follow-up 'Proving a Special Case of the Coxeter-Hadwiger Conjecture' (JAMP 2025, 13(8), 2700-2711), gives an algebraic proof that an n-dimensional Pythagorean simplex (i.e., an orthoscheme itself) can be trisected/dissected into n smaller orthoschemes of the same type. This is not a case of the stated conjecture in the sense that matters: the conjecture is about dissecting an arbitrary (general) simplex into orthoschemes, and the open frontier is dimension >= 6. Lénárt's starting object is already an orthoscheme, and the generalization of Coxeter's trisection of a path-simplex into n path-subsimplices for arbitrary dimension n was already established by Brandts, Korotov and Krizek in 2007 ('Dissection of the path-simplex in R^n into n path-subsimplices', Linear Algebra Appl.), well before the frozen revision date, so even read charitably as touching the conjecture's territory, this would be `open_stale`, not new progress. Because the scirp.org site returned 403 to automated fetching, I could not read the full abstract directly and relied on multiple independent search-result excerpts (consistent across four separate searches) describing the paper's actual content; I was unable to open the PDF or the paperinformation page myself. I found no mention anywhere of AI, machine learning, or automated theorem-proving involvement in any source touching this problem. I classify the record as open/no_change_found because no work in the window changed what a careful person would write about the stated conjecture (dissecting a general simplex, dimension >= 6 open).
competing_reading: One could argue the Lénárt papers deserve a `partial`/`open_stale` note rather than being folded entirely into 'no change', since they nominally invoke 'the Hadwiger Conjecture' in their titles and touch the same family of objects (orthoschemes, Coxeter trisection). But per the scope rule in §3.1, this is a related/variant construction (dissecting an already-orthoscheme simplex into orthoschemes) rather than a case of the stated question (dissecting a general simplex), and the underlying mathematical result it reproves predates the frozen revision by 17 years. I judged this insufficient to move the status off `open`, but flag the ambiguity since the triage pass's `found: []` did not surface these papers at all.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint claiming (with expert digestion) a bound f(6) for dissecting a general 6-dimensional simplex into finitely many orthoschemes, or a proof that no such finite bound exists in some dimension, would settle or move this record. Direct confirmation of the exact abstract text of the Lénárt papers (currently blocked by scirp.org's 403 response to automated fetchers) would also sharpen the classification, though based on consistent secondary descriptions I am confident it does not touch dimension >= 6 of the general conjecture.
